import torch


def quantize_int8(weight):
    """Per-tensor asymmetric signed INT8 quantization; return codes, scale, zero point.

    Include zero in the calibration range, so all-positive/all-negative constants
    remain representable. Dequantization is (codes.float()-zero_point)*scale.
    """
    if not weight.numel() or not torch.isfinite(weight).all():
        raise ValueError("expected finite nonempty weights")
    values = weight.float()
    minimum = min(float(values.min()), 0.0)
    maximum = max(float(values.max()), 0.0)
    scale = (maximum - minimum) / 255 if maximum != minimum else 1.0
    zero_point = max(-128, min(127, round(-128 - minimum / scale)))
    codes = (values / scale + zero_point).round().clamp(-128, 127).to(torch.int8)
    return codes, scale, zero_point
answer:
Affine INT8 maps real x to round(x/scale+zero_point), clips to [−128,127], and reconstructs with (q−zero_point)·scale. Include zero in the calibration range, especially for one-sided or constant tensors. This implementation uses one scale for the tensor; per-channel quantization can substantially reduce error when channels have different ranges. Stored codes alone do not accelerate inference without an appropriate integer kernel.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** Affine quantization uses $q=\operatorname{clip}(\operatorname{round}(x/s)+z,q_{min},q_{max})$ and $\hat x=s(q-z)$. Away from clipping, rounding error is at most roughly $s/2$. Calibration outliers enlarge $s$ and degrade resolution for ordinary values, motivating per-channel/group scales or other outlier-aware methods. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://newsletter.maartengrootendorst.com/p/a-visual-guide-to-quantization) and [2](https://leimao.github.io/article/Neural-Networks-Quantization/).
